title: How Much of a Harness Does a Strong Agent Need for Autonomous ML Engineering?
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:How Much of a Harness Does a Strong Agent Need for Autonomous ML Engineering?
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Recent autonomous machine learning engineering (MLE) agents have made significant progress on public leaderboards. Often motivated by progress stagnation over long-horizon cycles and limited Large Language Model (LLM) primitives, modern MLE agents are deployed on top of increasingly elaborate machinery: multi-agent orchestrators, dedicated retrieval subagents, and more. While such harnesses expand, the use of more primitive but improved coding agents - where LLMs have direct access to the execution environment through read, write, and bash primitives - has received little attention in the field. In this paper we find that, under an equal time budget and the same frontier LLM backbone, open-source state-of-the-art harnesses provide no advantages over a single session of a minimal-harness coding agent baseline, pointing to the backbone as the primary driver for performance. Via a series of large-scale systematic ablation studies, we argue that the machinery layers become redundant in the coding agent setting. We conclude that the effort spent elaborating hand-crafted harnesses around strong models yields poor returns for current MLE benchmarks.

report.summary: A new study finds that with the same strong LLM and equal time, elaborate agent harnesses offer no advantage over a minimal coding agent for autonomous ML engineering.
report.background: Autonomous ML engineering agents aim to handle long-horizon tasks such as data preparation, model training, hyperparameter tuning, and submission generation. As public leaderboards have become crowded, teams have built increasingly complex harnesses: multi-agent orchestrators, retrieval subagents, memory modules, and tool-routing layers. These designs assume that scaffolding compensates for LLM limitations and prevents stagnation over long runs. Separately, coding agents have improved: given read, write, and bash access, a strong model can inspect files, run experiments, and iterate directly. The paper tests whether the elaborate harness still matters when the underlying model is strong and time is held constant, a question with direct implications for agent architecture, compute budgets, and benchmark methodology.
key_points: Under an equal time budget and the same frontier LLM backbone, open-source state-of-the-art MLE harnesses showed no performance advantage over a single session of a minimal-harness coding agent. That controlled comparison suggests orchestration layers did not add measurable value on current benchmarks.

The LLM backbone appears to be the main performance driver. When the model is strong and can directly read, write, and run bash commands, extra agents and retrieval components mostly add complexity rather than capability. The finding reframes autonomous MLE as a model-capability problem more than a scaffolding problem.

Large-scale ablation studies found the machinery layers redundant in the coding-agent setting. Removing multi-agent orchestration and dedicated retrieval did not hurt outcomes, implying hand-crafted harnesses may duplicate capabilities the backbone already provides.

The authors argue that elaborate harness engineering yields poor returns for current MLE benchmarks. They recommend simpler baselines and caution that leaderboard gains may reflect backbone upgrades rather than harness design. This matters for how progress is reported and attributed.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the result challenges a prevailing 'scaffold-first' reflex. Teams may redirect engineering effort from bespoke multi-agent pipelines toward stronger base models, execution environments, and rigorous evaluation. Developers building agents should test minimal coding-agent baselines before adding orchestrators or retrieval subagents; simpler stacks are cheaper to maintain, easier to debug, and less brittle. Benchmark designers may need to report backbone, time budget, and baseline strength so harness gains are not overstated. For regular users, the practical effect could be more reliable and lower-cost autonomous tools, since fewer moving parts reduce failure modes. The caveat is scope: findings apply to current MLE benchmarks and equal-time settings, not necessarily to safety-critical, highly regulated, or collaborative workflows where specialized harnesses may still matter.
report.tools: Readers can follow MLE-bench for autonomous ML engineering evaluations, AIDE for ML engineering agent scaffolding, OpenHands and SWE-agent for coding-agent environments with bash/file access, and Aider for lightweight terminal-based coding workflows. When testing the paper's claim, compare a single minimal read/write/bash agent against a multi-agent harness under the same model and time budget. Track open-source minimal-agent baselines and reproducible ablation code rather than assuming more orchestration is better.
